Hyperliquid microstructure

Hypermirage: is liquidity on Hyperliquid's SP500 perp a mirage?

Partly. The displayed book is real and mostly stays put, even when prices jump. But it is thin where it counts: metaorders move the price 2 to 6 times more than the book implies, and depth falls to a third when CME futures pause.

@justinalick
market
xyz:SP500 perp, Hyperliquid
window
2026-10-08 to 2026-10-21 UTC
data
Hydromancer Reservoir / node data

Five things the order book says

  1. Liquidity runs on the CME clock, not the stock market's.Depth within 10 bps is $15.4M in US cash hours, $13.2M in other futures hours and $3.4M on weekends. A regime model finds nothing beyond that clock: session alone matches its split in 99.5% of minutes. depth · regimes
  2. Almost nothing on display ever trades.Only 0.28% of $1.08T in displayed notional filled. Half of 30M cancels are the same account re-quoting in the same block, mostly re-centering on a moved touch. cancels and amends
  3. Queue position decides who gets filled.Orders that improve the touch fill 14.5% of the time; orders joining behind $250k+ fill 3.2%. queue
  4. Small takers are early but still lose after fees.Takers pay 0.37 bps to cross, then the price follows them. Orders under $10k are ahead in 67% of hours at 10s, but at 1.13 bps in fees they end about 1 bp underwater. markouts
  5. Metaorders move price far more than the book suggests.Impact grows with size to the power 0.38, and metaorders move the price 2 to 6x more than walking the displayed book would. impact

Depth by hour and weekday

The daily CME break and weekends carry a quarter to a third of the depth of futures hours.

Finding. Liquidity runs on the clock of CME S&P 500 futures (ES), not the US cash session. Median depth within 10 bps is $15.4M in cash hours, $13.2M in other futures-open hours, $4.7M in the daily futures break (about 0.34x, a third of futures-open depth) and $3.4M on weekends (about 0.24x). The second chart shows the same data as one line over the week: it drops every weekday at 5pm ET when CME futures pause.

Caveats. Depth nets out partly filled orders and is within 2% of the exchange's one-minute snapshots 98.7% of the time. Those snapshots only reach about 3 bps from mid, so depth from 3 to 10 bps rests on the replay alone.

run ./run.sh analysis heatmap · analysis analysis/heatmap/depth_check.py · chart charts/heatmap.py, charts/depth_week.py · check checks/spotcheck/heatmap_depth_check.py

Book regimes

One session flag captures the book's regime; more states add noise.

Finding. The HMM finds one real regime, and it is the CME clock. The thin state ($3.6M within 10 bps, 0.38 bps spread) covers the daily ES halt and 99.5% of the weekend closure; the deep state ($13.9M, 0.14 bps) covers over 99% of cash and overnight hours. Session alone reproduces the 2-state split in 99.5% of minutes, stable across weeks (ARI 0.99).

Caveats. The third state is only a volatility label (5% vs 11.5% realized vol at the same depth) and is unstable (ARI 0.52 and 0.72 on week halves). The split holds with fill-adjusted depth, exchange L2 snapshots and with depth dropped entirely. Only two weekends.

run ./run.sh analysis regimes · analysis analysis/regimes/ · chart charts/regimes.py · check analysis/regimes/verify/

Depth vs volatility

Thin books here come from the clock, not from volatile minutes.

Finding. Depth follows the clock, not volatility. Across hours depth and volatility rise together (rho +0.63 over 336 hours), but within the same day and hour, volatile minutes carry about the same depth: -3.8% in cash hours, +4.8% overnight.

Caveats. The two weekends disagree and their exact figures are fragile (dropping orders that later filled moves -9% and -35% to 0% and -20%), so the chart shows them only as one weekend dropped and one did not. Two weekends are only two independent samples.

run ./run.sh analysis depth_vol · analysis analysis/depth_vol/, analysis/offhours/offhours_depth.py · chart charts/depth_vol.py · check checks/spotcheck/depth_vol_verify.py

Volatility, spread and depth

When volatility rises, makers widen their quotes rather than pull size.

Finding. Volatility widens the spread but does not thin the book. Comparing each one-minute snapshot with the same UTC hour on the same day, the most volatile tenth of minutes while CME futures are open has a median time-weighted quoted spread 19% wider than the calmest tenth (day-bootstrap 90% CI: +15% to +24%), while depth within 10 bps of mid is unchanged (-1%, 90% CI -5% to +2%).

Caveats. Spread is time-weighted between one-minute snapshots from the replayed book, and an independent recompute matches within 0.1 pp. While futures are closed both series are noisy, and there are only two weekends of data. The 1-minute L2 snapshots show the same widening in the mean spread (+22%, against +30% for the replayed book on the same measure); the headline +19% uses medians, which the snapshots cannot show because they sit at one tick 92% of the time.

run ./run.sh analysis vol_spread · analysis analysis/vol_spread/ · chart charts/vol_spread.py · check checks/vol_spread/check_vol_spread.py

Maker concentration

About a third of maker volume rests on three accounts, and which three changes day to day.

Finding. The top three maker accounts supply 36.0% of maker volume over the 14 days pooled, and 34% to 46% on individual days (median 38.8%). Merging declared sub-accounts barely changes it (36.1%); Oct 18 is the only day that shifts, from 38% to 44%.

Caveats. Daily shares sit above the pooled share because the leading accounts rotate. Only sub-account links declared on Hyperliquid were merged. Accounts that could be looked up cover 95.5% of maker volume.

run ./run.sh analysis concentration · analysis analysis/concentration/, charts/concentration_cache.py · chart charts/concentration.py · check checks/spotcheck/verify_concentration.py

Order survival

Near the touch, a quote is usually gone within a second: latency and re-quoting dominate resting size.

Finding. Most quotes near the touch are cancelled within a second: 65% of orders at or inside the touch and 72% of orders up to 1 bp behind it, against 26% of orders more than 5 bps away. 26.0M displayed orders from 2,914 accounts.

Caveats. Blocks are converted to seconds with each day's own block time, and 31 orders with no measurable distance are excluded. Few orders fill or stay open, so the cancel-share bounds sit within 0.6 points.

run ./run.sh analysis survival · analysis charts/survival_cache.py, analysis/survival_viz.py · chart charts/survival.py · check checks/spotcheck/survival_verify.py

Cancels and amends

Most fast cancels are quotes re-centering on a moved touch, not liquidity leaving.

Finding. Only 0.28% of the notional of 26M resting orders ever filled. Half of the 30M cancels are same-block replacements by the same account and side (23% identical, 17% price only, usually 1 to 3 ticks). After the touch moves, near-touch orders are pulled 1.7 to 3.3 times faster by 1s, mostly quotes re-centering.

Caveats. Displayed lifetime is partly an outcome, since filled orders stop resting when they fill. A native modify and a cancel plus new order look the same in these data. Behavior only, not intent.

run ./run.sh analysis cancels · analysis analysis/cancels/ · chart charts/cancels_1.py, charts/cancels_2.py, charts/cancels_3.py · check checks/cancels/

Queue position and fills

Queue position at entry matters more than order size: improving the touch fills four times as often.

Finding. Queue position matters. Orders that improve the touch fill 14.5% of the time, orders joining behind at most $5k 12.7%, and orders joining behind more than $250k 3.2%. Holding own size at $5k to $15k the drop is steeper, 10.8% to 1.3%. 2.75M touch orders, Oct 9 to 21, from a FIFO replay where 95.8% of maker fills hit the replayed queue head.

Caveats. The median order lives under a second, so these odds mostly measure how fast makers cancel. Queue position is measured at entry only, volatility is not controlled for, and the time panel past about 5s rests on under 15% of orders.

run ./run.sh analysis queue · analysis analysis/queue_replay.py, analysis/queue_fill.sql, analysis/queue_km.py · chart charts/queue_fill.py · check checks/queue/

Fill markouts

Small takers are early, but on small orders the fee is larger than the edge.

Finding. Takers pay about 0.37 bps to cross, then the price follows them: the pooled taker markout turns positive after about 5 seconds and reaches about +0.17 bps at 2 to 5 minutes. Orders under $10k are ahead in 55% of hours at 1s and 67% at 10s; orders of $100k and over pay the most to cross and get back to about break-even only after a minute or more.

Caveats. All markouts are gross of fees. The average taker fee of 0.78 bps includes builder fees (exchange fee alone 0.58 bps). Orders under $10k pay 1.13 bps, so their +0.16 bps at 1 minute is about 1 bp underwater after fees. The mid is taken as of every top-of-book change, so the 0.5s and 1s points are exact; the real limit is replay accuracy (98.6% of taker fills at or through the replayed touch). An independent recompute matched every mean within 0.00004 bps. The violin axis clips 30 hourly values; arrows count them.

run ./run.sh analysis markouts · analysis analysis/markout/rerun/ · chart charts/markouts.py, charts/markouts_violin.py · check checks/spotcheck/markout_rerun_verify_markouts.py

Price impact

The visible book understates what metaorders cost by 2 to 6x.

Finding. Impact is concave but not a clean square root. Fitted exponents are about 0.38 [0.30, 0.43] for metaorders and 0.39 for single taker orders. The prefactor Y is driven by one account: 1.45 for the largest taker against 0.55 for everyone else. Metaorders move the price 2 to 6 times more than walking the displayed book (about 5 to 6x under $10k, about 3x at $50k to $300k, 1.7 to 3x at $450k to $1M).

Caveats. The 0.44 and 0.29 exponents on the left panel are per-group fits; the pooled figures are above. Single orders move the mid less than the book implies only from about $45k up. Q/V reaches only about 7e-3, small metaorders partly chase momentum, and Y moves from 0.52 to 0.85 with the metaorder gap rule alone.

run ./run.sh analysis impact · analysis analysis/impact/ · chart charts/impact.py · check checks/spotcheck/impact_verify.py

Metaorder shapes

The number of child orders matters more for impact than how they are spread over time.

Finding. Execution shape separates metaorders only weakly. Only a 3-way split is stable (bootstrap ARI median 0.81, week to week 0.64): front-loaded (3,885), spread out (6,479) and back-loaded (3,029) of 13,393 metaorders with 4+ child orders. 81% of native TWAPs land in spread out. Impact Y for accounts other than the largest taker is 1.02, 0.68 and 1.23, with overlapping CIs.

Caveats. Child-order count drives Y more than shape (0.28 for single orders, about 1 for 4+), which points at how metaorders are defined rather than how they are executed. The back-loaded edge is partly mechanical, time shape cannot see icebergs, and 53% of clustered metaorders come from one account.

run ./run.sh analysis metaorders · analysis analysis/metaorder_shapes/ · chart charts/metaorder.py · check checks/spotcheck/metaorder_shapes_verify.py

Taker markouts by cluster

The largest taker is close to break-even against makers; a few small takers lead the price more per dollar.

Finding. The largest taker (T1, 29% of taker notional) leads the price only slightly: +0.17 bps at 1s, +0.32 at 10s and +0.38 at 60s, against -0.16, -0.09 and +0.02 for all other takers. It pays about 0.30 bps in taker fees (others about 0.98), leaving it near break-even. Its share tracks ES hours: 34% in cash hours, 27% overnight, 8% when ES is closed.

Caveats. Without ES prices, no lead-lag test against the futures was possible. Per dollar, two much smaller takers show larger markouts (+1.6 and +1.8 bps at 60s). The 21 UTC bar also includes Friday's close. Only 5% of taker notional sits in multi-address clusters.

run ./run.sh analysis taker_clusters · analysis analysis/taker_clusters/ · chart charts/taker_markouts.py · check analysis/taker_clusters/verify.sql

Order flow imbalance

Order flow describes the move but does not forecast it at a size that survives spread and fees.

Finding. OFI explains same-bin price moves well but barely predicts the next one. With the slope refit every half hour, median same-bin R-squared rises from 15% at 1s to 57% at 1m; at 10s it is 50% in US cash hours against 17% outside. Out-of-sample next-bin R-squared is 1.3% at 1s and zero or negative from 10s on.

Caveats. Predicted moves are far below the half-spread plus fees, so nothing here is tradable. The 1s edge is mostly speed and falls to 0.1% with a 1s delay. Book sizes matched only 65% of snapshots on Sun Oct 11.

run ./run.sh analysis ofi · analysis analysis/ofi/ · chart charts/ofi.py · check checks/spotcheck/ofi_verify.py

Funding and the oracle premium

The discount to the oracle is a CME-hours effect; funding is small next to it.

Finding. The perp trades about 3 bps below the oracle only while CME futures are open: about -3.2 bps while ES trades against -0.05 bps over the 1,645 hours it is closed. The median premium is -2.5 bps and is negative in 78% of hours. Funding is too small to matter: a constant long collected 0.67% over the period, about 1.1% a year.

Caveats. Deep discounts do not reliably predict a bounce. The most discounted fifth of hours was followed by +27 bps over 24h, but that comes from March and April; the non-overlapping daily test gives a correlation of -0.10 over 207 days (t = -1.46). Funding pays shorts only when the premium is below -3 bps.

Different sample: Mar 18 to Oct 23, 2026 from the public API (5,255 funding hours; 4,978 hours with a 24h forward return after removing a duplicate candle), not the 14-day window.

run ./run.sh analysis funding · analysis analysis/funding/ · chart charts/funding.py · check checks/funding/recompute.py

Do traders form archetypes? Mostly no

Clusters of traders mostly dissolve when tested against shuffled data.

Finding. Archetypes mostly do not hold up. Only two clusters come close to stable: 69 fast post-only quoters (2s median rest, 62% of notional, Jaccard 0.71) and 114 slower post-only makers (15s rest, 2% of notional, 0.73). The large API-taker group scores 0.41 and builder-routed clusters 0.1 to 0.2. The picture is one maker block plus a continuum of takers.

Caveats. Median bootstrap ARI is 0.25. HDBSCAN on the raw features finds nothing in 85 of 200 resamples, and the same pipeline finds islands in shuffled data, so most apparent structure is order-type plumbing. 1,487 accounts with at least 30 fills.

UMAP axes have no units; they place accounts that behave alike close together, and UMAP can draw tight islands even in noise, which is why the shuffled-data panel is the control.

run ./run.sh analysis archetypes · analysis analysis/archetypes/ · chart charts/archetypes_v2.py

Methods and data

Fills and order statuses for the xyz:SP500 perp on Hyperliquid, Oct 8 to 21, 2026, from Hydromancer Reservoir / node data; funding and oracle premium from the Hyperliquid public API, Mar 18 to Oct 23, 2026. The order book is replayed block by block (about 70 ms) from node order statuses and checked against exchange snapshots. Markouts use the mid as of every top-of-book change; confidence intervals are block bootstraps over hours. Every headline number was recomputed with separate code; most sections link an independent check script. Accounts are addresses, not firms, and nothing here identifies one. The charts describe measured behavior, not intent.

Replicate it. All code is at github.com/justinalick/hypermirage (pinned to commit 6354f71); each section above links its own analysis and chart scripts, and most link an independent check script. Reservoir data is a requester-pays S3 bucket, and node data needs Hydromancer access; see the repo README.

Thanks to Hydromancer for the Reservoir and node data behind every chart on this page.

git clone https://github.com/justinalick/hypermirage && cd hypermirage
./run.sh fetch       # Reservoir fills + 1-minute L2
./run.sh pipeline    # per day: order lifecycle and block-by-block book replay
./run.sh analysis    # every topic, or e.g. ./run.sh analysis markouts
./run.sh charts      # the charts on this page, in out/
./run.sh checks      # independent recomputes of the published numbers
